subject: BBIS
stem: The Bombay (Oh) phenotype is defined by the absence of which antigen on red cells?
explanation: Bombay individuals (hh) cannot make H antigen, the precursor of A and B, so they have no A, B, or H antigens and produce anti-A, anti-B, and anti-H. Reference: Dean, Blood Groups and Red Cell Antigens, The Hh blood group (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK2268).
choice_notes: A and B are also missing, but the defining loss is H.
A and B are also missing, but the defining loss is H.
No H (FUT1 defect), so A and B cannot be made; plasma has anti-H.
Rh antigen; unrelated to the Bombay phenotype.

subject: BBIS
stem: Anti-D produced after exposure to D-positive red cells is mostly of which immunoglobulin class?
explanation: Immune anti-D is mainly IgG. That is why it can cross the placenta and cause hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN). Reference: Dean, Blood Groups and Red Cell Antigens, Hemolytic disease of the newborn (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK2266).
choice_notes: Seen first in a primary response, but immune anti-D is mostly IgG.
Warm IgG that crosses the placenta, so it causes HDFN.
Not the class of red cell alloantibodies.
Involved in allergy, not red cell antibodies.

subject: BBIS
stem: Which test detects red cells that were sensitized with antibody or complement in vivo?
explanation: The DAT tests the patient's red cells directly for bound IgG or complement (in vivo sensitization). The IAT detects in vitro sensitization. Reference: StatPearls, Rh Blood Group System (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK594252).
choice_notes: Detects antibody in the serum, sensitized in vitro.
AHG added to washed patient cells shows in-vivo coating (HDFN, AIHA, reactions).
Uses the IAT to find antibodies in serum.
Checks ABO compatibility only; no AHG phase.

subject: BBIS
stem: Which immunoglobulin is the first to appear in a primary immune response?
explanation: IgM appears first in a primary response. IgG dominates the secondary (anamnestic) response. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 18.4 B Lymphocytes and Humoral Immunity (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/18-4-b-lymphocytes-and-humoral-immunity).
choice_notes: First made in a primary response; a pentamer.
Rises later and dominates the secondary response.
Mainly in secretions.
Mostly on naive B cells as a receptor.

subject: BBIS
stem: Platelet concentrates are stored at:
explanation: Platelets are kept at room temperature (20–24 °C) with continuous gentle agitation to keep them viable. Cold storage causes them to lose function. Reference: Platelet Storage: Problems, Improvements, and New Perspectives, section 3.1 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11277025).
choice_notes: Red cell storage temperature; cold makes platelets clump and lose function.
Room temperature with agitation keeps platelets working; shelf life about 5 days.
Plasma storage temperature.
Too warm; bacteria would grow.

subject: BBIS
stem: Which of these syphilis tests is nontreponemal?
explanation: RPR and VDRL are nontreponemal tests. TP-PA, FTA-ABS, and EIAs/CIAs detect antibodies to Treponema pallidum itself. A presumptive diagnosis needs one test of each kind. Reference: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines, Syphilis (cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/syphilis.htm).
choice_notes: Treponemal test (detects antibody to T. pallidum).
Treponemal test; stays positive for life.
Detects antibody to cardiolipin (reagin), not to the treponeme itself.
Treponemal test.

subject: BBIS
stem: Which syphilis test is used to monitor the response to treatment?
explanation: Nontreponemal titers usually fall and often become nonreactive after successful treatment, so they are followed over time; treponemal tests usually stay reactive. Titers from RPR and VDRL can't be compared directly. Reference: CDC STI Treatment Guidelines, Syphilis (cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/syphilis.htm).
choice_notes: Titers fall with successful treatment; a fourfold drop is significant.
Treponemal; usually stays positive after treatment.
Treponemal; usually stays positive after treatment.
Treponemal; usually stays positive after treatment.

subject: BBIS
stem: The most frequent cause of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction is:
choices: ABO incompatibility from a clerical error or patient misidentification
explanation: Most acute hemolytic reactions come from ABO-incompatible blood given because of a clerical error or wrong patient identification. Anti-IgA causes anaphylaxis, and overload is TACO. Reference: What every physician should know about transfusion reactions (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1913131); StatPearls, ABO Blood Group System (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK580518).
choice_notes: Causes fever and shock (septic reaction), less common.
Wrong patient or wrong unit is the main cause; IgM anti-A/B lyses cells.
Causes anaphylaxis, not hemolysis.
TACO; not hemolytic.

subject: BBIS
stem: Rh immune globulin should be given to a D-negative mother who delivered a D-positive baby within:
explanation: RhIG is given within 72 hours of delivery (with a routine dose at 26–28 weeks) to prevent anti-D. A standard 300 µg dose covers about 15 mL of fetal red cells; a Kleihauer-Betke test guides extra doses for larger bleeds. Reference: StatPearls, Rho(D) Immune Globulin (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557884) and Kleihauer-Betke Test (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430876).
choice_notes: Within the window, but not the outer limit.
Give as soon as possible, within 72 hours of delivery.
Too late for the standard dose window.
Antenatal dose is given at about 28 weeks, a different timing.

subject: BBIS
stem: Ulex europaeus lectin has which specificity?
explanation: Ulex europaeus is the anti-H lectin. Dolichos biflorus is the anti-A1 lectin. Reference: A Study of A1 and A2 Subtypes Among Whole-Blood Donors With Blood Groups A and AB (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11046175).
choice_notes: Dolichos biflorus is anti-A1.
Bandeiraea simplicifolia is anti-B.
Detects H; reacts most with group O cells.
Vicia graminea is anti-N; not an M lectin.

subject: BBIS
stem: Forward typing: anti-A 0, anti-B 4+. Reverse typing: A1 cells 4+, B cells 0. The blood group is:
explanation: The cells carry B antigen (react with anti-B only), and the serum has the expected naturally occurring anti-A (agglutinates A1 cells). This is group B. Reference: ABO blood groups and galectins: Implications in transfusion medicine and innate immunity (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11808837).
choice_notes: Would react with anti-A and have anti-B.
B antigen on cells, anti-A in plasma.
Would react with both antisera and neither reverse cell.
Would react with neither antiserum and both reverse cells.

subject: BBIS
stem: Compared with A1 cells, A2 red cells react MORE strongly with:
explanation: A2 cells convert H to A inefficiently, so more H remains and they react more strongly with anti-H. Dolichos biflorus agglutinates A1 but not A2 cells. Reference: A Study of A1 and A2 Subtypes Among Whole-Blood Donors With Blood Groups A and AB (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11046175).
choice_notes: A2 converts less H to A, so more H remains.
A2 cells do NOT react with anti-A1.
Not related to A subgroups.
Rh antigen; unrelated.

subject: BBIS
stem: Dolichos biflorus lectin is used to identify:
explanation: The anti-A1 lectin of Dolichos biflorus agglutinates A1 red cells but not A2 red cells. Reference: A Study of A1 and A2 Subtypes Among Whole-Blood Donors With Blood Groups A and AB (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11046175).
choice_notes: Agglutinates A1 cells but not A2.
Use Ulex europaeus.
Not a B lectin.
Not an M lectin.

subject: BBIS
stem: The immunodominant sugar of the A antigen is:
explanation: The A transferase adds N-acetyl-D-galactosamine and the B transferase adds D-galactose to H substance. H itself is formed by adding fucose. Reference: A Study of A1 and A2 Subtypes Among Whole-Blood Donors With Blood Groups A and AB (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11046175); ABO blood groups and galectins: Implications in transfusion medicine and innate immunity (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11808837).
choice_notes: The immunodominant sugar of H.
The immunodominant sugar of B.
A transferase adds it to H.
Part of the precursor chain, not the A sugar.

subject: BBIS
stem: A group A secretor will have which blood group substances in saliva?
explanation: In group A secretors, A and H antigens are found in saliva. The FUT2 (Se) gene encodes the fucosyltransferase used in secretions. Reference: Use of a recombinant deacetylase to convert A1 red blood cells to the acquired B phenotype (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10920065); ABO blood groups and galectins: Implications in transfusion medicine and innate immunity (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11808837).
choice_notes: A secretor also secretes H, the precursor.
Se gene lets H and A appear in secretions.
Group O secretors have only H.
That is a nonsecretor.

subject: BBIS
stem: The "acquired B" phenomenon is associated with:
choices: Group A1 persons with certain bacterial infections
explanation: Bacterial enzymes can change the A sugar into a B-like structure, so group A1 cells react weakly with anti-B. The change stops once the infection clears. Reference: Use of a recombinant deacetylase to convert A1 red blood cells to the acquired B phenotype (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10920065).
choice_notes: Not the usual setting.
Not the usual setting.
Bacterial deacetylase turns A sugar into one like B (e.g., colon cancer, gut infection).
Not the usual setting.

subject: BBIS
stem: The universal donor for PLASMA is group:
explanation: Group AB serum contains neither anti-A nor anti-B, so AB plasma can be given to any ABO group. For red cells, group O is the universal donor. Reference: ABO blood groups and galectins: Implications in transfusion medicine and innate immunity (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11808837).
choice_notes: Group O plasma has anti-A and anti-B; O is the red cell universal donor.
Has anti-B.
Has anti-A.
AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B.

subject: BBIS
stem: Anti-A and anti-B antibodies develop naturally:
choices: During the first few months of life
explanation: ABO antibodies develop naturally during the first few months of life, which is why reverse typing is not reliable in newborns. Reference: ABO blood groups and galectins: Implications in transfusion medicine and innate immunity (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11808837).
choice_notes: Newborns have little or no ABO antibody of their own.
Start at about 3–6 months from exposure to similar antigens in gut bacteria.
They are present without any transfusion.
They are present without pregnancy.

subject: BBIS
stem: Weak D differs from partial D because weak D has:
choices: Fewer D antigen sites (a quantitative change)
explanation: Weak D is a quantitative weakening of the D antigen. In partial D, single epitopes of D are lost, so these persons can form anti-D. Reference: Flegel, The genetics of the Rhesus blood group system, Blood Transfus 2007 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2535884).
choice_notes: Normal D epitopes but fewer of them; usually does not make anti-D.
That describes partial D.
That describes D-negative.
Not the definition.

subject: BBIS
stem: The most immunogenic Rh antigen is:
explanation: Of the Rh antigens, D is the most immunogenic, which is why D-negative persons get D-negative blood and RhIG in pregnancy. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 19.1 Hypersensitivities (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/19-1-hypersensitivities).
choice_notes: Less immunogenic than D.
Very immunogenic; most D-negative people exposed make anti-D.
Less immunogenic than D.
Less immunogenic than D.

subject: BBIS
stem: An Rh-null phenotype can result from a defect in which gene needed for Rh protein expression?
explanation: Rh-null red cells lack Rh antigens; one cause is a defect in the RHAG gene, whose protein is needed for Rh proteins to reach the membrane. Reference: Flegel, The genetics of the Rhesus blood group system, Blood Transfus 2007 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2535884).
choice_notes: RHAG is needed to carry Rh proteins to the membrane.
Controls A and B transferases.
Controls H antigen (Bombay when absent).
Kell blood group gene.

subject: BBIS
stem: The Kleihauer-Betke test is used to:
choices: Estimate the volume of fetomaternal hemorrhage
Determine the ABO group of the fetus
explanation: The Kleihauer-Betke test estimates how much fetal blood entered the mother, which guides the RhIG dose. Reference: FIGO/ICM guidelines for preventing Rhesus disease: A call to action (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7898700).
choice_notes: Acid elution removes adult Hb; fetal cells with HbF stay pink.
Not its purpose.
Weak D is tested with IAT.
That is antibody identification.

subject: BBIS
stem: Rh antigens are carried on:
choices: Plasma proteins adsorbed onto the cells
Transmembrane proteins encoded by RHD and RHCE
explanation: The Rh antigens are on two membrane proteins, RhD and RhCE, each crossing the membrane 12 times, encoded by RHD and RHCE on chromosome 1. Reference: Flegel, The genetics of the Rhesus blood group system, Blood Transfus 2007 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2535884).
choice_notes: Those carry ABO, Lewis and P antigens.
Lewis antigens are adsorbed from plasma.
Carry MN antigens.
Nonglycosylated proteins that cross the membrane many times.

subject: BBIS
stem: One full-dose vial (300 micrograms) of Rh immune globulin protects against a fetomaternal hemorrhage of about:
explanation: One 1500 IU (300 microgram) dose of anti-D is enough to neutralize 30 mL of fetal whole blood. Reference: FIGO/ICM guidelines for preventing Rhesus disease: A call to action (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7898700).
choice_notes: Too small.
That is the volume of packed red cells covered (15 mL).
Covers about 30 mL of fetal whole blood (15 mL red cells).
Too large; more vials would be needed.

subject: BBIS
stem: Persons with a partial D phenotype:
choices: Can make anti-D against the D epitopes they lack
explanation: In partial D, single epitopes of the D antigen are lost, so these persons can form anti-D after exposure to normal D. Reference: Flegel, The genetics of the Rhesus blood group system, Blood Transfus 2007 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2535884).
choice_notes: Missing parts of D, so exposure to normal D can trigger anti-D.
They can make anti-D.
They usually type D-positive.
That is Rh-null.

subject: BBIS
stem: For transfusion, a patient with a partial D phenotype is usually typed and managed as:
choices: Weak D, so any blood is safe
explanation: Partial D patients are treated as D-negative for transfusion to avoid anti-D, but as D-positive when they donate. Reference: Integrating RHD Genotyping for More Accurate Rh(D) Antigen Phenotyping (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12028936).
choice_notes: Treated as D-negative to avoid anti-D formation.
Risk of making anti-D if given D-positive blood.
Rh-null lacks all Rh antigens.
Partial D is not weak D, and it can still make anti-D.

subject: BBIS
stem: The leading cause of the D-negative phenotype worldwide is:
explanation: Deletion of the RHD gene is the leading cause of the D-negative phenotype; a person homozygous for the deletion is D-negative. Reference: Flegel, The genetics of the Rhesus blood group system, Blood Transfus 2007 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2535884).
choice_notes: Most D-negative Europeans have no RHD gene.
Causes Rh-null, which is rare.
Weak D types as D-positive with enough reagents.
RHCE codes C, c, E and e, not D.

subject: BBIS
stem: In an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, the post-reaction direct antiglobulin test (DAT) is usually:
explanation: The DAT is usually positive, except rarely when all incompatible red cells have already been destroyed. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf).
choice_notes: Donor cells coated with antibody give a positive DAT, unless they are already lysed.
Usually positive, though it can be negative if all coated cells are destroyed.
It is a key test in the reaction workup.
No anti-IgE AHG test exists for this.

subject: BBIS
stem: In cold agglutinin disease, the DAT may also be weakly positive for IgG in up to about:
explanation: The DAT is typically strongly positive for C3d; weak IgG positivity is seen in up to 20% of cases. Reference: Berentsen, Cold agglutinin disease, Hematology Am Soc Hematol Educ Program 2016 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6142439).
choice_notes: Up to about 20% may also show weak IgG.
Too high; most cases show C3d only.
Some cases do show weak IgG.
Too high.

subject: BBIS
stem: Polyspecific AHG reagent contains:
explanation: The polyspecific antiglobulin reagent contains both anti-IgG and anti-complement (C3), so it detects either on red cells. Reference: Berentsen, Cold agglutinin disease, Hematology Am Soc Hematol Educ Program 2016 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6142439).
choice_notes: Not in polyspecific AHG.
That is monospecific anti-IgG.
Detects both antibody and complement on cells.
Not in AHG reagent.

subject: BBIS
stem: In cold agglutinin disease, the DAT is typically positive with:
explanation: In cold agglutinin disease the DAT is positive for C3d, with IgG negative or only weakly positive. Reference: The role of serological and molecular testing in the diagnostics and transfusion treatment of AIHA (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9256513); Berentsen, Cold agglutinin disease, Hematology Am Soc Hematol Educ Program 2016 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6142439).
choice_notes: Seen in warm AIHA.
IgM cold antibody fixes complement, then falls off, leaving C3d.
The DAT is positive.
Not typical.

subject: BBIS
stem: An elution procedure is used to:
choices: Remove antibody bound to red cells so it can be identified
explanation: In elution, antibodies are separated from the red cells so they can be shown and identified in the eluate. Reference: Flegel, The genetics of the Rhesus blood group system, Blood Transfus 2007 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2535884).
choice_notes: Not the purpose.
That is sensitization.
Freed antibody (eluate) is then identified with panel cells.
Not the purpose.

subject: BBIS
stem: Red blood cell units are stored at:
explanation: Red-cell-containing components are stored at 1 to 6 C. Conventional platelets are kept at 20 to 24 C. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf).
choice_notes: Platelet storage temperature.
Keeps red cells for up to 35–42 days, depending on the solution.
Plasma storage temperature.
Too warm.

subject: BBIS
stem: Fresh frozen plasma is stored frozen at:
explanation: FFP is frozen at -18 C or colder. After thawing it is kept at 1 to 6 C and used within 24 hours. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf).
choice_notes: Red cell storage temperature.
Platelet storage temperature.
Frozen within 8 hours of collection; keeps up to 1 year.
Too warm.

subject: BBIS
stem: Red cells collected in CPDA-1 expire after:
explanation: CPDA-1 gives red cells a shelf life of 35 days (adenine supports ATP). Red cells in additive solutions last 42 days. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf).
choice_notes: Red cells in additive solutions (e.g., AS-1) last 42 days.
CPD or ACD red cells last 21 days.
Platelet shelf life.
Adenine helps red cells make ATP, extending storage.

subject: BBIS
stem: Cryoprecipitate is a source of:
choices: Fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF and factor XIII
explanation: Cryoprecipitated AHF contains fibrinogen, factor VIII, factor XIII and vWF. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf).
choice_notes: Made by thawing FFP at 1–6 °C; used for low fibrinogen.
Albumin and IVIG come from fractionation.
Factor IX and VII are in plasma, not cryo.
Platelets are a separate component.

subject: BBIS
stem: Blood components are irradiated mainly to prevent:
explanation: Irradiation makes donor T lymphocytes unable to proliferate, preventing transfusion-associated graft-vs-host disease. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf).
choice_notes: Leukocyte reduction helps prevent these.
Kills donor T cells so they cannot attack the recipient.
Leukocyte reduction or CMV-negative units lower this risk.
Washing or antihistamines help with these.

subject: BBIS
stem: Leukocyte reduction lowers the risk of all of the following EXCEPT:
explanation: Leukocyte-reduced components lower febrile reactions, CMV transmission and HLA alloimmunization, but they do not prevent TA-GVHD; irradiation does. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf).
choice_notes: Reduced, since white cell cytokines cause fever.
Reduced, since fewer HLA-bearing white cells are given.
Reduced, since CMV lives in white cells.
Only irradiation prevents TA-GVHD; a few T cells can still remain.

subject: BBIS
stem: Washed red cells may be used for patients with:
choices: IgA deficiency with anti-IgA, or severe repeated allergic reactions
explanation: Washing removes plasma proteins, so it can be used for IgA-deficient recipients or patients with repeated anaphylactic reactions to plasma. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf).
choice_notes: Treated with iron, not washed cells.
Treated with factor VIII.
Washing removes plasma proteins such as IgA.
Needs platelets.

subject: BBIS
stem: Irradiated red cells, compared with nonirradiated ones, have higher:
explanation: Irradiated red cells have higher supernatant potassium, so their expiration date is shortened. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf).
choice_notes: Radiation damages red cell membranes, so potassium leaks out.
Red cell units contain almost no platelets.
Not in red cell units in any useful amount.
Not in red cell units in any useful amount.

subject: BBIS
stem: One whole-blood-derived platelet unit should raise the platelet count of a 70-kg adult by about:
explanation: One whole-blood-derived platelet unit raises a 70-kg adult's count by 5,000 to 10,000/uL; an apheresis unit by about 30,000 to 60,000/uL. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf).
choice_notes: Too small.
An apheresis unit raises it by about 30,000–60,000/µL.
Closer to an apheresis unit's increase.
Too large.

subject: BBIS
stem: A temperature rise of at least 1 C during transfusion with no signs of hemolysis is most likely a:
explanation: A febrile nonhemolytic reaction is a temperature rise of 1 C or more (or chills) during or within 4 hours of transfusion with no other cause. Hemovigilance defines fever as 38 C or higher. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf); CDC NHSN Biovigilance Component, Hemovigilance Module Protocol (cdc.gov/nhsn/pdfs/biovigilance/bv-hv-protocol-current.pdf).
choice_notes: Hemolysis would show a positive DAT, hemoglobinuria and so on.
White cell cytokines cause fever; leukoreduction prevents it.
Shows acute lung injury within 6 hours.
Shows hypotension and breathing problems, no fever.

subject: BBIS
stem: Severe anaphylaxis after only a few mL of plasma in an IgA-deficient patient is due to:
explanation: Anaphylactic reactions have been reported in IgA-deficient patients with anti-IgA, although most anaphylactic reactions have no identifiable cause. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf).
choice_notes: IgA-deficient patients can make anti-IgA; give IgA-deficient or washed products.
Causes TRALI.
Causes delayed hemolytic reactions.
Causes fever and shock.

subject: BBIS
stem: Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is most often caused by:
explanation: TRALI is hypoxemia with noncardiogenic pulmonary edema within 6 hours of transfusion, most often from donor white-cell antibodies. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf).
choice_notes: That causes anaphylaxis.
Antibodies in donor plasma activate the recipient's neutrophils in the lung.
That is TACO.
That is a septic reaction.

subject: BBIS
stem: New respiratory distress with evidence of volume overload after a large or rapid transfusion suggests:
explanation: TACO is cardiogenic pulmonary edema from transfusing too much volume or too fast. Patients with heart or kidney disease and the elderly are at risk. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf).
choice_notes: Fever with no volume overload.
Hives and itching.
Lung injury without fluid overload; antibody-mediated.
Too much volume too fast; often high blood pressure; responds to diuretics.

subject: BBIS
stem: Delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions usually occur how long after transfusion?
explanation: In previously alloimmunized patients, an anamnestic antibody response destroys the transfused cells, usually 2 to 14 days after transfusion. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf).
choice_notes: That is an acute reaction.
Anamnestic response from an earlier exposure (often Kidd antibodies).
Too late.
That is an acute reaction.

subject: BBIS
stem: The FIRST thing to do when a transfusion reaction is suspected is to:
choices: Stop the transfusion and keep the IV line open with saline
explanation: If a hemolytic reaction is suspected, the transfusion must be stopped and the transfusion service notified immediately. Reference: AABB et al., Circular of Information for the Use of Human Blood and Blood Components, June 2024 (weareblood.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Circular-of-Information-for-the-Use-of-Human-Blood-and-Blood-Components-June-2024.pdf).
choice_notes: Workup comes after stopping.
Never continue a suspected reaction.
Stopping limits exposure; saline keeps IV access for treatment.
Not the first step.

subject: BBIS
stem: ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn most often occurs in infants of mothers who are group:
explanation: ABO HDFN is caused by maternal IgG anti-A and/or anti-B, and occurs in group A or B infants of group O mothers. Reference: Recommendations for the prevention and treatment of haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn, Blood Transfus 2015 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4317097).
choice_notes: Less likely; anti-B is mostly IgM.
Less likely; anti-A is mostly IgM.
Has no anti-A or anti-B.
Group O people have IgG anti-A,B that crosses the placenta.

subject: BBIS
stem: Kernicterus in severe HDFN results from:
explanation: Kernicterus is permanent brain damage from very high unconjugated bilirubin. Phototherapy and exchange transfusion lower the risk. Reference: The Spectrum of Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn: Evaluating the Etiology of Unconjugated Hyperbilirubinemia (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8418802).
choice_notes: Unconjugated bilirubin is fat-soluble and crosses the blood-brain barrier.
Water-soluble; does not enter the brain.
Not the cause.
Not the cause.

subject: BBIS
stem: Which immunoglobulin is the only one that crosses the placenta?
explanation: IgG is the only antibody class that can cross the placenta, which is why it protects the newborn and can cause HDFN. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 18.1 Overview of Specific Adaptive Immunity (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/18-1-overview-of-specific-adaptive-immunity).
choice_notes: Does not cross the placenta.
Too large to cross the placenta.
Crosses the placenta through FcRn receptors.
Does not cross the placenta.

subject: BBIS
stem: Which immunoglobulin is secreted as a pentamer and is the most efficient at agglutination?
explanation: Secreted IgM is a pentamer with 10 binding sites, which makes it the most efficient antibody for agglutination. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 18.1 Overview of Specific Adaptive Immunity (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/18-1-overview-of-specific-adaptive-immunity).
choice_notes: A monomer; works best at 37 °C with AHG.
Ten binding sites make it the best at agglutination and complement fixation.
Usually a dimer in secretions.
A monomer.

subject: BBIS
stem: Which immunoglobulin predominates in tears, saliva and breast milk?
explanation: Secretory IgA is the most abundant antibody class in mucus secretions and is also found in breast milk, tears and saliva. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 18.1 Overview of Specific Adaptive Immunity (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/18-1-overview-of-specific-adaptive-immunity).
choice_notes: Secretory IgA is a dimer that protects mucous membranes.
Mainly a B-cell receptor.
Allergy antibody.
Main antibody in serum, not secretions.

subject: BBIS
stem: Which antibody binds to mast cells and basophils in type I hypersensitivity?
explanation: The Fc region of IgE binds to mast cells and basophils; allergen cross-linking triggers histamine release. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 18.1 Overview of Specific Adaptive Immunity (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/18-1-overview-of-specific-adaptive-immunity).
choice_notes: Type II and III reactions.
Type II and III reactions.
Not involved.
Cross-linked IgE makes mast cells release histamine.

subject: BBIS
stem: The classical complement pathway begins when which component binds to antigen-antibody complexes?
explanation: IgG or IgM bound to an antigen recruits and activates the C1 complex (through C1q), starting the classical pathway. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 18.1 Overview of Specific Adaptive Immunity (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/18-1-overview-of-specific-adaptive-immunity); Berentsen, Cold agglutinin disease, Hematology Am Soc Hematol Educ Program 2016 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6142439).
choice_notes: Part of all pathways, but not the starting component.
Binds antibody Fc and starts the classical pathway.
Part of the alternative pathway.
Starts the lectin pathway.

subject: BBIS
stem: Complement activation that continues through C5 ends with formation of the:
explanation: Activation of C5 leads to formation of the membrane attack complex, which makes pores and lyses cells. Reference: Berentsen, Cold agglutinin disease, Hematology Am Soc Hematol Educ Program 2016 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6142439).
choice_notes: C5b–C9 makes pores in the cell membrane.
Antigen bound to antibody.
Presents antigen; not part of complement.
Starts the classical pathway.

subject: BBIS
stem: MHC class II molecules present antigen to:
explanation: Helper T cells (CD4) are activated by antigen presented with MHC II; cytotoxic T cells (CD8) recognize antigen with MHC I. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 18.3 T Lymphocytes and Cellular Immunity (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/18-3-t-lymphocytes-and-cellular-immunity).
choice_notes: Class I presents to CD8 cells.
Class II is on antigen-presenting cells (macrophages, B cells, dendritic cells).
NK cells kill cells that lack class I.
Not antigen-presenting targets.

subject: BBIS
stem: Which hypersensitivity type is T cell-mediated (delayed), as in the tuberculin skin test?
explanation: Type IV hypersensitivity reactions are T cell-mediated, delayed reactions. Types I to III are antibody-mediated. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 19.1 Hypersensitivities (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/19-1-hypersensitivities).
choice_notes: IgE-mediated allergy.
Antibody against cell antigens (e.g., transfusion reactions).
Immune complex disease (e.g., serum sickness).
T cells react 48–72 hours later.

subject: BBIS
stem: A small molecule that becomes immunogenic only when bound to a larger carrier protein is a(n):
explanation: A hapten is too small to trigger a response alone; it must first attach to a larger carrier molecule, usually a protein. Reference: OpenStax Microbiology, 18.1 Overview of Specific Adaptive Immunity (openstax.org/books/microbiology/pages/18-1-overview-of-specific-adaptive-immunity).
choice_notes: Boosts the immune response but is not the antigen.
The part of an antigen an antibody binds.
Too small to trigger antibodies alone.
Stimulates many lymphocytes regardless of specificity.

subject: BBIS
stem: A false-negative agglutination result due to antibody excess is called:
explanation: Prozone happens when excess unbound antibody causes false-negative reactions. Diluting the serum can resolve it. Reference: High Titer Antibodies Demonstrating Prozone in Two Repeat Blood Donors (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10064354).
choice_notes: Antigen excess.
Best lattice formation and strongest reaction.
Too much antibody blocks lattice formation; dilute and retest.
Coin stacking from high protein, not true agglutination.

subject: BBIS
stem: Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titers help support a diagnosis of:
choices: Post-streptococcal disease such as rheumatic fever
explanation: ASO measures antibodies to streptolysin O of group A strep and shows a past or recent strep infection, which supports post-strep complications such as rheumatic fever. Reference: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia, Antistreptolysin O titer (medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003522.htm).
choice_notes: Antibody to a group A strep toxin; shows recent strep infection.
Use the Monospot test.
Use RPR, VDRL or treponemal tests.
Use HBV serology.

subject: BBIS
stem: The Monospot test detects heterophile antibodies in:
explanation: Mono tests (heterophile antibody tests) are used for infectious mononucleosis, most often caused by Epstein-Barr virus. Reference: MedlinePlus Lab Tests, Mononucleosis (Mono) Tests (medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mononucleosis-mono-tests).
choice_notes: CMV gives a heterophile-negative mononucleosis.
Use the rheumatoid factor test.
Heterophile antibodies agglutinate sheep or horse red cells.
Use syphilis tests.

subject: BBIS
stem: Which hepatitis B marker indicates recent infection (within about 6 months)?
explanation: IgM anti-HBc positivity indicates recent hepatitis B infection (less than 6 months) and acute infection. Reference: CDC, Interpretation of Hepatitis B Serologic Test Results (cdc.gov/hepatitis-b/media/serologicchartv8.pdf).
choice_notes: Shows immunity.
IgM to the core antigen marks an infection within about 6 months.
Not a usual marker of recent infection.
IgM anti-HBc is the marker.

subject: BBIS
stem: A person vaccinated against hepatitis B who was never infected is positive only for:
explanation: HBsAg negative, anti-HBc negative and anti-HBs positive means immune due to hepatitis B vaccination. Anti-HBc appears only after natural infection. Reference: CDC, Interpretation of Hepatitis B Serologic Test Results (cdc.gov/hepatitis-b/media/serologicchartv8.pdf).
choice_notes: Means current infection.
Means past or current infection.
Means active viral replication.
The vaccine has only HBsAg, so only anti-HBs forms.

subject: BBIS
stem: C-reactive protein is:
choices: An acute-phase protein made by the liver
A protein made by plasma cells
explanation: The liver makes CRP in response to inflammation, and its level rises and falls with the amount of inflammation. Reference: MedlinePlus Lab Tests, C-Reactive Protein (CRP) Test (medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/c-reactive-protein-crp-test).
choice_notes: Rises within hours of inflammation, infection or injury.
That is ASO.
Not part of complement, though it can activate it.
Made by the liver.

subject: BBIS
stem: In the CDC laboratory HIV testing algorithm, the recommended initial test is a(n):
explanation: CDC recommends starting with an HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody combination immunoassay; reactive results go to an antibody differentiation assay. Western blot is no longer used. Reference: CDC & APHL, Laboratory Testing for the Diagnosis of HIV Infection: Updated Recommendations, 2014 (stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/23447).
choice_notes: No longer used in the CDC algorithm.
4th-generation test detects p24 antigen and antibodies, so it finds infection earlier.
Shows immune status, not infection.
Not used for routine diagnosis.

subject: BBIS
stem: Rheumatoid factor is a protein made by the immune system that attacks:
explanation: Rheumatoid factor is made by the immune system and attacks the body's own immunoglobulin G (IgG). Reference: MedlinePlus Lab Tests, Rheumatoid Factor (RF) Test (medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/rheumatoid-factor-rf-test).
choice_notes: That is antinuclear antibody (ANA).
That is antiphospholipid antibody.
Usually IgM against the Fc part of IgG.
That is ASO.
